questions.q: The incident ray, reflected ray and the outward drawn normal are denoted by the unitvectors $\overset{\to}{a}, \overset{\to}{b}$and $\overset{\to}{c}$ respectively. Then choose the correct relation for these vectors.
questions.solution:
$\overset{\to}{a} = sin\theta\overset{^}{i} - cos\theta\overset{^}{j}$

$\overset{\to}{b} = sin\theta\overset{^}{i} + cos\theta\overset{^}{j}$

$\overset{\to}{c} = \overset{^}{j}$

$\overset{\to}{a} - 2\left(\overset{\to}{a} \cdot \overset{\to}{c}\right)\overset{\to}{c} = sin\theta\overset{^}{i} + cos\theta\overset{^}{j}$

questions.q: For a concave lens of focal length $f$, the relation between object and image distance $u$ and $v,$ respectively, from its pole can best be represented by ($u = v$ is the reference line):
questions.solution:
From the lens formula, $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$⇒ v = f - \dfrac{{f}^{2}}{u + f}$

now, if we plot a graph between $u\text{and}v$

When $u \to \infty ; v = f - \dfrac{{f}^{2}}{\infty} = f$

and for $u \to 0; v = 0$

Given that $u = v$is a reference line, therefore, $\dfrac{d v}{d u} = 0 + \dfrac{{f}^{2}}{{\left(u + f\right)}^{2}}$

${\dfrac{d v}{d u}}_{u = 0} = 0 + \dfrac{{f}^{2}}{{\left(0 + f\right)}^{2}} = 1$

The equation of tangent of the curve at the origin, $v - 0 = 1\left(u - 0\right) ⇒ v = u$

questions.q: Time taken by light to travel in two different materials $A$ and $B$ of refractive indices ${\mu}_{A}$ and ${\mu}_{B}$ of same thickness is ${t}_{1}$ and ${t}_{2}$ respectively. If ${t}_{2} - {t}_{1} = 5 \times {10}^{- 10}s$ and the ratio of ${\mu}_{A}$ to ${\mu}_{B}$ is $1: 2$. Then the thickness of material, in meter is: (Given ${v}_{A}$ and ${v}_{B}$ are velocities of light in $A$ and $B$ materials respectively).
questions.solution:
The speed of light in a medium is inversely proportional to the refractive index of the material. Therefore,

$\dfrac{{\mu}_{A}}{{\mu}_{B}} = \dfrac{{v}_{B}}{{v}_{A}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Let the thickness is $d$

$⇒ {t}_{2} - {t}_{1} = \dfrac{d}{{v}_{B}} - \dfrac{d}{{v}_{A}} = 5 \times {10}^{- 10}s$

As ${v}_{A} = 2{v}_{B} ⇒ d = 5 \times {10}^{- 10} \times 2{v}_{B}$

$⇒ d = 5 \times {10}^{- 10} \times {v}_{A}m$.

questions.q: A convex lens has power $P$. It is cut into two halves along its principal axis. Further one piece (out of the two halves) is cut into two halves perpendicular to the principal axis (as shown in figures). Choose the incorrect option for the reported pieces.
questions.solution:
Using Lens maker's formula, power is given by

$P = \dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\mu - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{{R}_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{{R}_{2}}\right)$

When convex lens is cut into two parts, ${P}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\mu - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{2}{R}\right) = P$

When half convex lens is cut into two parts,${P}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\mu - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R}\right) = \dfrac{P}{2}$

Power of lens, ${P}_{3} = \dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\mu - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R}\right) = \dfrac{P}{2}$

questions.q: A $2$ meter long scale with least count of $0 . 2cm$ is used to measure the locations of objects on an optical bench. While measuring the focal length of a convex lens, the object pin and the convex lens are placed at $80cm$ mark and $1m$ mark, respectively. The image of the object pin on the other side of lens coincides with image pin that is kept at $180cm$ mark. The $%$ error in the estimation of focal length is:
questions.solution:
The formula for a lens is given by $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} . . . ( i )$

$u = \left(100 \pm 0 . 2\right)cm - \left(80 \pm 0 . 2\right)cm = \left(20 \pm 0 . 4\right)cm$

$v = \left(180 \pm 0 . 2\right)cm - \left(100 \pm 0 . 2\right)cm = \left(80 \pm 0 . 4\right)cm$

Substituting the values in the equation of focal length,

$\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{80} - \left(- \dfrac{1}{20}\right) = \dfrac{5}{80}$

$⇒ f = 16cm$

Differentiating the equation (i)

$\dfrac{df}{{f}^{2}} = \dfrac{dv}{{v}^{2}} + \dfrac{du}{{u}^{2}}$(Only positive sign is considered for error calculation)

$= \dfrac{0 . 4}{6400} + \dfrac{0 . 4}{400} = 0 . 4 \times \dfrac{17}{6400}$

$⇒ df = 0 . 4 \times \dfrac{17}{6400} \times {16}^{2} = 0 . 272$

The percentage error is

$\dfrac{df}{f} \times 100 = \dfrac{0 . 272}{16} \times 100 = 1 . 70 %$

questions.q: An ice cube has a bubble inside. When viewed from one side the apparent distance of the bubble is $12cm$. When viewed from the opposite side, the apparent distance of the bubble is observed as $4cm$. If the side of the ice cube is $24cm$, the refractive index of the ice cube is
questions.solution:
Let's assume that the original position of the bubble is $x$ from one side of the ice cube of side $a$.

When the bubble is seen from one side, it can be written that

$\dfrac{x}{\mu} = 12 . . . \left(1\right)$

For the view from the other side, it can be written that

$\dfrac{a - x}{\mu} = 4 . . . \left(2\right)$

From equations (1) and (2), it is given that

$\begin{cases}24 - 12\mu & = & 4\mu \\ & ⇒ & \mu = \dfrac{24}{16} \\ & = & 1 . 5\end{cases}$

questions.q: A beam of plane polarized light of large cross-sectional area and uniform intensity of $3 .3 W{m}^{– 2}$ falls normally on a polarizer (cross-sectional area $3 \times {10}^{– 4}{m}^{2}$), which rotates about its axis with an angular speed of $31 .4 rad{s}^{- 1}$. The energy of light passing through the polarizer per revolution, is close to:
questions.solution:
Given,

Intensity of plane polarized light of large cross-sectional area is ${I}_{0} = 3 . 3W{m}^{- 2}$

Area of cross-section of polarizer is $A = 3 \times {10}^{- 4}{m}^{2}$

Angular speed of rotation is $\omega = 31 . 4rad{s}^{- 1}$

The intensity of light is the given by the definition,

$I = \dfrac{E}{AT} . . . ( 1 )$

Intensity of light passing through the polarizer as polarizer rotates is given by

${I}_{avg} = {I}_{0}\dfrac{1}{T}{∫}_{0}^{T}\cos^{2}\left(\omegat\right) d t$

$⇒ {I}_{avg} = {I}_{0}\dfrac{1}{T}{∫}_{0}^{T}\left[\dfrac{1 + cos\left(2\omegat\right)}{2}\right] d t$

$⇒ {I}_{avg} = {I}_{0}\dfrac{1}{2T}\left[{∫}_{0}^{T} d t + {∫}_{0}^{T}cos\left(2\omegat\right) d t\right]$

$⇒ {I}_{avg} = {I}_{0}\dfrac{1}{2T}\left[T + 0\right]$

$⇒ {I}_{avg} = \dfrac{{I}_{0}}{2} . . . ( 2 )$

Using equation (1) and (2) we get energy per revolution is given by

$E = \dfrac{{I}_{0}A}{2}T = \dfrac{{I}_{0}A}{2}\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$

$E = \dfrac{3 .3 \times 3 \times {10}^{- 4}}{2}\dfrac{3 . 14}{31 . 4}$

$E ≃ 1 \times {10}^{- 4}J$

questions.q: Two coherent sources of light interfere. The intensity ratio of two sources is $1: 4$. For this interference pattern if the value of $\dfrac{{I}_{max} + {I}_{min}}{{I}_{max} - {I}_{min}}$ is equal to $\dfrac{2\alpha + 1}{\beta + 3}$, then $\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}$ will be
questions.solution:
Given here, $\dfrac{{I}_{1}}{{I}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ or ${I}_{2} = 4{I}_{1}$

Maximum intensity is ${I}_{max} = {\left(\sqrt{{I}_{1}} + \sqrt{{I}_{2}}\right)}^{2} = {I}_{1} + 4{I}_{1} + 2\sqrt{{I}_{1}4{I}_{1}} = 9{I}_{1}$

Minimum intensity is ${I}_{min} = {\left(\sqrt{{I}_{1}} - \sqrt{{I}_{2}}\right)}^{2} = {I}_{1} + 4{I}_{1} - 2\sqrt{{I}_{1}4{I}_{1}} = {I}_{1}$

The ratio of $\dfrac{{I}_{max} + {I}_{min}}{{I}_{max} - {I}_{min}}$ is

$\dfrac{9{I}_{1} + {I}_{1}}{9{I}_{1} - {I}_{1}} = \dfrac{10}{8} = \dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{2\alpha + 1}{\beta + 3}$

$\alpha = 2\beta = 1$

$∴ \dfrac{\alpha}{\beta} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2$

questions.question: Two coherent sources of light interfere. The intensity ratio of two sources is $1: 4$. For this interference pattern if the value of $\dfrac{{I}_{max} + {I}_{min}}{{I}_{max} - {I}_{min}}$ is equal to $\dfrac{2\alpha + 1}{\beta + 3}$, then $\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}$ will be
questions.explanation:
Given here, $\dfrac{{I}_{1}}{{I}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ or ${I}_{2} = 4{I}_{1}$

Maximum intensity is ${I}_{max} = {\left(\sqrt{{I}_{1}} + \sqrt{{I}_{2}}\right)}^{2} = {I}_{1} + 4{I}_{1} + 2\sqrt{{I}_{1}4{I}_{1}} = 9{I}_{1}$

Minimum intensity is ${I}_{min} = {\left(\sqrt{{I}_{1}} - \sqrt{{I}_{2}}\right)}^{2} = {I}_{1} + 4{I}_{1} - 2\sqrt{{I}_{1}4{I}_{1}} = {I}_{1}$

The ratio of $\dfrac{{I}_{max} + {I}_{min}}{{I}_{max} - {I}_{min}}$ is

$\dfrac{9{I}_{1} + {I}_{1}}{9{I}_{1} - {I}_{1}} = \dfrac{10}{8} = \dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{2\alpha + 1}{\beta + 3}$

$\alpha = 2\beta = 1$

$∴ \dfrac{\alpha}{\beta} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2$

questions.q: ‘$n$’ polarizing sheets are arranged such that each makes an angle $45 °$ with the proceeding sheet. An unpolarized light of intensity $I$ is incident into this arrangement. The output intensity is found to be $\dfrac{I}{64}$ . The value of $n$ will be:
questions.solution:
When an unpolarized light passes through a polariser, the intensity of the emergent light from the polariser depends on the square of the cosine of the angle between the plane of the polariser and the direction of the incident light.

The formula to calculate the intensity $\left({I}_{1}\right)$ of the emergent light from a polariser which makes an angle $\theta$ with the direction of the incident light is given by

${I}_{1} = I\cos^{2}\theta . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 1 )$

where, $I$ is the intensity of the incident light.

Substitute $45 °$ for $\theta$ into equation (1) to obtain the intensity of the first emergent light.

$\begin{cases}{I}_{1} & = & I\cos^{2}45 ° \\ & = & \dfrac{I}{2}\end{cases}$

In a similar manner, the intensity $\left({I}_{2}\right)$ of the second emergent light can be written as

$\begin{cases}{I}_{2} & = & {I}_{1}\cos^{2}45 ° \\ & = & \dfrac{{I}_{1}}{2} \\ & = & \dfrac{I}{4} \\ & = & \dfrac{I}{{2}^{2}}\end{cases}$

Thus, for $n$ number of such polarisers, the net intensity $\left({I}_{n}\right)$ of the emergent light can be written as

${I}_{n} = \dfrac{I}{{2}^{n}} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 1 )$

Comparing equation (1) with the given expression for the intensity, it can be concluded that

$n = 6$
